title: Classics close: your shelf
hookLine: pick the five books you'll reread for life
tomorrow: Lumen Gentium 11: a page number, a chapter, or something else?

lines: A BOX, AND ONE SMALL SHELF.
cards: A moving box sits open on the floor. The new room has one small shelf: room for five books, no more. Not the books you ought to have read, or the ones that look good to guests.
Five you'd take down again years from now, on a hard night, and open anywhere. A hand hovers over the pile, and stops. This block of short classics ends right there, at that box.

teach.b: First, look back at the shelf this block built. Brother Lawrence, flipping an omelette for the love of God. Julian of Norwich, and love as his meaning.
Catherine of Siena's bridge. Then the oldest voices: the Didache's prayer, Ignatius of Antioch's anvil, Polycarp, Justin's Sunday, Perpetua's ladder.
The desert monk who said become all flame, Antony laughing, Patrick's breastplate, Benedict's tools, Bernard, Anselm, Hildegard, Francis.
And this last stretch: Clare, Teresa, John, Ignatius the pilgrim, Francis de Sales, Newman, Hopkins, Chesterton.
Second, how several of them began: a letter to one sister, a rule for one house, a story told to a companion, a poem written on a stuck ship.
Written to someone, and that may be part of why they still read like someone talking to you. Third, why reread.
These writers knew about going back. Ignatius's life turned on a book handed to him on a sickbed. Clare told Agnes to keep looking.
Teresa's garden needs watering again and again. A book you return to reads a little differently each time, because you've changed. Fourth, the answer to the box.
Five, not fifty. Some from this block, some from anywhere.
The test isn't greatness; it's the hard night.
Which ones would you open then? Not a ranking. A shelf.

how: Some Catholics keep a small shelf of spiritual classics for regular rereading, and lectio divina, the slow, prayerful reading of a text, is one way they return to them.

games.q: your grandmother is moving into a small room and can take only a few books. your cousin says take the fancy matching set. what does the block's shelf ask?
o: which ones she'd open on a hard night, whatever they look like.
which ones look best on the shelf for visitors.
which ones are the most important books ever written.
games.why: not a ranking and not a display: books to keep opening, the way these writers knew about going back.

practice: On a piece of paper, write the numbers one to five down the side. Let titles come, from this block or from anywhere in your life, and keep only the ones you'd open again on a hard night.
If you pray, give thanks for whoever first put those books in your hands.

wordCard.voice: Classics close. The end of a block of short classics, from the earliest letters to Chesterton, and a shelf of your own to keep. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin for reading, as in lectio divina: slow, prayerful reading, made for books you return to.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: five books, chosen for the hard night and not for the guests. See you in the documents.
